newsitem.title: USA: Clinton defends welfare reform, and fund-raising.
newsitem.headline: Clinton defends welfare reform, and fund-raising.

text.p: President Bill Clinton ran into some criticism of his welfare reform plans on Tuesday on a visit to New York where he was also raising more than $1 million to help elect Democrats to the Senate.

At a roundtable discussion at the Riverside Church near Harlem on Manhattan's West Side, Clinton defended his efforts to get people off welfare rolls by offering tax credits and other incentives for businesses that hire people off welfare.

Earl Graves, chief executive officer of Black Enterprise Magazine, reflected some frustration at Clinton's decision last summer to sign a Republican-backed welfare reform law that ended a 61-year federal entitlement to welfare.
He said the law was "designed to destroy" the government's social safety net but that "government cannot and must not abandon its role."

"It is unrealistic and unfair to expect the private sector in general and black-owned businesses in particular to sacrifice profit margins in order to do the government's job," Graves said. "Unlike the federal government, we can go out of business."

Clinton bristled at the criticism and heatedly defended his proposals in support of his second-term goal of getting 1 million people off welfare in the next four years. He said government was still providing a safety net.
"Let me say, with all due respect, I don't think it's that simple," he said. "I don't think it's accurate to say that this bill destroys the safety net for poor people."

He said the federal government alone will not be able to reduce the welfare rolls, that charitable organisations and employers must help too and that cities and states must get the money he has proposed for reforming welfare. Clinton has proposed $750 million for the budget year starting Oct. 1 for new welfare-to-work initiatives.
"This can be done and I need your help to do it. I think it's part of all our mission in life to do this," he said.

Nilda Roman, who has been on welfare for the last three years, complained of the lack of training that poor people like herself receive for employment, and talked of the demeaning way these people are treated.
"We don't mind. But it's the way we're treated when we get there," she said. "I've seen the women clean the toilets. It's horrid and it's demeaning."

Clinton got a reminder of the other main purpose of his trip to New York -- fund-raising -- on the motorcade drive into town. A ticker tape electronic billboard advertising Fairway supermarkets said, "Hey Mr. President ... Fairway coffee 35 cents a cup ... White House coffee $200,000 a cup and our tastes so much better..."

At a time when Democratic fund-raising practices from last year's campaigns are under investigation, Clinton was going to the home of a wealthy donor, Shelby Bryan, on the Upper East Side to raise more than $1 million from 120 people.
In his remarks to them, he planned to encourage Democrats not to be scared away from contributing to the party at a time when it has been called into question.
The fund-raiser occurred less than a month after he ballyhooed a new voluntary ban on gifts from foreign nationals and contributions over $100,000 at the Democratic National Committee.

Those rules did not apply to this event, because it was sponsored by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, and it has not adopted the new DNC regulations. The White House wants the Senate committee and its House counterpart to adopt the rules but does not feel it can dictate to them.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said there was a witch hunt atmosphere in Washington that all fund-raisers were bad and urged reporters to be fair.
"Unless the argument here is that we go to public financing and taxpayers pay for politics, there will be fund-raisers in the future. Candidates will have to raise money."
Republicans who outspent Democrats by far last year are busily replenishing their coffers as well.

Some 200 Republican big spenders -- members of the party's exclusive "Team 100" -- will be spending three days shmoozing, golfing, playing tennis and sunbathing with Republican officials and congressional leaders, including House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, at a posh Palm Beach, Fla., hotel resort this week.

Don Simon, executive vice president of Common Cause, seeking campaign finance reform, told Reuters the Democratic and Republican fundraising operations show that "basically we've got a system in a state of total collapse and I think both parties are taking full advantage of it. There's kind of an anything goes attitude -- just raise as much as you can from whomever you can in whatever amounts you can get."
